content_html:
A desktop workbench for making CAD parts with an AI coding agent.
You point at the part. The agent writes the code. torno builds it every time you save.

Getting started · Manual · How it works · Contributing

Note

torno is new and early. It is developed on Linux (Arch, Wayland) 100% using claudecode and also runs on macOS, which has seen less use. Expect rough edges, and please open an issue when you find one.

Why torno

Coding agents are good at writing build123d models, the Python CAD library on top of OpenCascade. Two things get in the way. The agent can't see what it made, and it's hard for you to tell it which face is wrong, or by how much.

torno fixes both. It runs Claude Code next to a live 3D view of the model. You pin a note to a face, measure a wall or draw on the view, and the agent gets exactly what you pointed at: the face's ref, the exact measured value, your note. The agent also gets tools to look at the model, measure it and cut sections through it, so it can check its own work before it hands it back.

torno is not a modeller. It has no feature tree and no way to edit a solid by hand, and its sketches tell Claude what you mean rather than make geometry. The model is the Python file, and torno shows it.

Features

  • Live builds. Every save rebuilds the model and redraws it. When a build fails, the last good parts stay on screen and the traceback is one click away. A failed fillet tells you which edges and what radius would work.
  • Point, don't describe. Pins, arrows, strokes, shapes and picks on faces and edges, each with a note. The agent gets them with your next prompt as refs like lid/F12, never as vague words. What you have selected waits in a tag by the part, with what the kernel says of it.
  • What waits on you. The top of the left column says how the build on show stands (2 checks fail, 5 pass) and lists what needs you: a failing check, Claude's question, a mark to review. Parameters and Parts are two tabs under it, and Ctrl+P finds any part or value in a model of many. Ctrl+Shift+L hides the column.
  • Sketch in 3D. Draw strokes in space, on a plane or on the surface of the parts, in millimetres, to show where something goes or how it runs. More
  • Review a build. Go over a build once, marking what you don't want and what you want, and send it as one round. Claude answers each item, and after the next build you say OK or Still wrong. More
  • Name what you mean. Give a few faces, edges, parts or strokes a name like #deck that you and Claude both use. torno finds them again after every build. More
  • Every build kept. The builds timeline under the view groups them by prompt and lets you compare two builds, star one, review one, or go back to before a prompt.
  • Exact numbers. Distances, angles, radii and wall thickness are measured on the B-rep, not on the mesh. Give a dimension the value it should be and it says passes or fails after every build.
  • The agent sees what you see. The agent gets MCP tools of its own: look (a picture of your view, marks included), measure, section, check (overlaps and printability), diff between builds, try_fillet and more.
  • Section, explode, saved views. Cut through the parts, pull an assembly apart, keep a camera under a name.
  • Scans. Import a phone or scanner mesh of the place the part has to fit, align it, and check clashes and deviation against it. torno always marks scan numbers as approximate. A scan is a tab beside Model and Brief.
  • Tracings. Lay one plane of the model flat at true size on a millimetre grid, over a photo of the real thing if you have one. The outline is redrawn after every build. It is a tab of the same switch. More
  • A brief for each project. One page with what you are making, the sizes you know and where each came from, the rules, the photos and notes, and your checks, dimensions and marks. Claude is told the sizes and rules in every new conversation. More
  • Start from what you have. A new project can start from a description, photos, doodles, scans and other projects in the workspace. Claude gets all of it with its first prompt. All your projects stand on one bench at true scale, the ones waiting on you first.
  • Export. A single HTML file anyone can open in a browser without installing anything, or STEP, STL and 3MF, a PNG of the view, and an SVG or PDF drawing of a section or a tracing at true scale.
  • Local. torno itself uploads nothing. The agent is your own claude, under your own login, and torno leaves its settings alone. In your folders, torno writes only under <project>/.torno/, and a session can edit files only in its own project.

A 3D sketch Reviewing a build A tracing

What goes well, and what does not

It goes well with prismatic parts that have sizes you measured: brackets, enclosures, holders, a lid and a box, hole patterns. It needs more from you for a part that must fit a place you can only scan, and for an assembly of more than three or four parts that touch. It does not go well with organic shapes described in words alone, gears and threads written by hand, or sizes read from a photo. Whatever the part, give a measured number, a scan or a dimension mark in place of a description. The manual has the lists.

How it works

A workspace is a folder of projects. Each project is a folder with one build123d model in it:

projects/
├── bracket/
│   └── bracket.py
└── hollow/
    └── hollow.py

A model gives its parts as a dict, or as make_<part>() functions, or as module-level shapes:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from build123d import Box, Cylinder, Pos

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Params:
    side: float = 40
    wall: float = 2

def assembly(p):
    inner, height = p.side - 2 * p.wall, p.side - p.wall
    tub = Pos(0, 0, height / 2) * Box(p.side, p.side, height)
    tub -= Pos(0, 0, p.wall + inner / 2) * Box(inner, inner, inner)
    tub += Pos(0, 0, p.wall + 10) * Cylinder(3, 20)
    lid = Pos(0, 0, height + p.wall / 2) * Box(p.side, p.side, p.wall)
    return {"tub": tub, "lid": lid}

The app is Electron and three.js. The kernel is a Python package that loads models and tessellates them in forked workers. Each project gets its own Claude Code session, in the project's folder, connected to torno's MCP server on 127.0.0.1. See Projects and builds for the full rules.

Getting started

Requirements

  • Linux or macOS (not Windows: the launcher, the terminal view and the login-shell PATH are for Unix; WSL2 is untried)
  • Node.js 22.12 or later, and pnpm 10
  • uv (it fetches Python 3.11 or 3.12 if you have neither)
  • Claude Code (claude) on your PATH, logged in

torno checks all of this on its first screen, under "Ready to work", and says what's missing. The first build sets up torno's own Python environment with build123d and bd_warehouse (about 900 MB, once). If your workspace has its own pyproject.toml, torno uses that environment instead and never changes it. Run uv sync there once yourself. More in Requirements.

Install

git clone https://github.com/luisg0nc/torno.git
cd torno
pnpm install

Run

scripts/torno ~/projects    # open a folder as the workspace
scripts/torno               # the workspace you opened last, or the first screen

The launcher rebuilds the app when the sources change, so git pull and run it again. On the first screen, Open the example opens a small project, an enclosure with its brief and a few marks, in a temporary copy, so you can try everything without touching your own files.

On Linux, scripts/torno --install-desktop adds torno to your application launcher, or pnpm dist:linux builds an AppImage and a tar.gz in app/dist/. On macOS, pnpm dist:mac builds torno.app in app/dist/ (signed ad hoc, not notarized). More in Run.

Your first five minutes

Press Open the example on the first screen. It is an enclosure for a sensor board, with a lid that rattles. The manual has a walk-through on it: turning, pinning, measuring, cutting and asking the agent to fix the fit. It works the same from a packaged app.

Working with Claude Code in torno

A few habits that save time.

  • Point, don't describe. Pin the face and write the note. The agent gets the face's ref and your words, not "the left side near the top".
  • Give measured sizes. Put what you have measured in the brief or the first prompt. A size the agent guesses is the usual reason a part does not fit.
  • Make a dimension a standing test. Measure the wall or the gap, type the value it should have, and it says passes or fails after every build, whoever made the change.
  • Ask for two or three rough blockouts before details. Compare the shapes first. Fillets and holes can wait.
  • Ask for measured sizes back. "What is the wall under the lid?" is answered from the B-rep, exactly. Say so when you want the number and not a look.
  • Run /mcp__torno__review before you call it done. The agent goes through every open mark and every unmet dimension against the current build.
  • One project, a few parts. Split a big assembly into projects. Use saved views to come back to the same angle.

The manual says what the agent is given and told.

Documentation

  • The manual, the reference for everything torno does. The parts most people need:
    • The agent: the chat, what Claude Code is given and told, the tools
    • Marks and measuring
    • Scans and export
    • Keys, files torno writes, troubleshooting
  • The design, why torno is built the way it is.

Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome. torno is young, so for anything bigger than a fix, please open an issue first to talk it over. CONTRIBUTING.md covers setting up, where things are, the rules the code holds to, and the tests. Questions and parts you made go in Discussions. To report a security problem, see SECURITY.md.

content_html_zh:
A desktop workbench for making CAD parts with an AI coding agent. You point at the part. The agent writes the code. torno builds it every time you save.

Getting started · Manual · How it works · Contributing

Note

torno is new and early. It is developed on Linux (Arch, Wayland) 100% using claudecode and also runs on macOS, which has seen less use. Expect rough edges, and please open an issue when you find one.

Why torno

Coding agents are good at writing build123d models, the Python CAD library on top of OpenCascade. Two things get in the way. The agent can't see what it made, and it's hard for you to tell it which face is wrong, or by how much.

torno fixes both. It runs Claude Code next to a live 3D view of the model. You pin a note to a face, measure a wall or draw on the view, and the agent gets exactly what you pointed at: the face's ref, the exact measured value, your note. The agent also gets tools to look at the model, measure it and cut sections through it, so it can check its own work before it hands it back.

torno is not a modeller. It has no feature tree and no way to edit a solid by hand, and its sketches tell Claude what you mean rather than make geometry. The model is the Python file, and torno shows it.

特征

  • Live builds. Every save rebuilds the model and redraws it. When a build fails, the last good parts stay on screen and the traceback is one click away. A failed fillet tells you which edges and what radius would work.
  • 点，不描述。 Pins, arrows, strokes, shapes and picks on faces and edges, each with a note. The agent gets them with your next prompt as refs like lid/F12, never as vague words. What you have selected waits in a tag by the part, with what the kernel says of it.
  • What waits on you. The top of the left column says how the build on show stands (2 checks fail, 5 pass) and lists what needs you: a failing check, Claude's question, a mark to review. Parameters and Parts are two tabs under it, and Ctrl+P finds any part or value in a model of many. Ctrl+Shift+L hides the column.
  • Sketch in 3D. Draw strokes in space, on a plane or on the surface of the parts, in millimetres, to show where something goes or how it runs. More
  • Review a build. Go over a build once, marking what you don't want and what you want, and send it as one round. Claude answers each item, and after the next build you say OK or Still wrong. More
  • Name what you mean. Give a few faces, edges, parts or strokes a name like #deck that you and Claude both use. torno finds them again after every build. More
  • Every build kept. The builds timeline under the view groups them by prompt and lets you compare two builds, star one, review one, or go back to before a prompt.
  • Exact numbers. Distances, angles, radii and wall thickness are measured on the B-rep, not on the mesh. Give a dimension the value it should be and it says passes or fails after every build.
  • The agent sees what you see. The agent gets MCP tools of its own: look (a picture of your view, marks included), measure, section, check (overlaps and printability), diff between builds, try_fillet and more.
  • Section, explode, saved views. Cut through the parts, pull an assembly apart, keep a camera under a name.
  • Scans. Import a phone or scanner mesh of the place the part has to fit, align it, and check clashes and deviation against it. torno always marks scan numbers as approximate. A scan is a tab beside Model and Brief.
  • Tracings. Lay one plane of the model flat at true size on a millimetre grid, over a photo of the real thing if you have one. The outline is redrawn after every build. It is a tab of the same switch. More
  • A brief for each project. One page with what you are making, the sizes you know and where each came from, the rules, the photos and notes, and your checks, dimensions and marks. Claude is told the sizes and rules in every new conversation. More
  • Start from what you have. A new project can start from a description, photos, doodles, scans and other projects in the workspace. Claude gets all of it with its first prompt. All your projects stand on one bench at true scale, the ones waiting on you first.
  • 出口。 A single HTML file anyone can open in a browser without installing anything, or STEP, STL and 3MF, a PNG of the view, and an SVG or PDF drawing of a section or a tracing at true scale.
  • Local. torno itself uploads nothing. The agent is your own claude, under your own login, and torno leaves its settings alone. In your folders, torno writes only under <project>/.torno/, and a session can edit files only in its own project.

What goes well, and what does not

It goes well with prismatic parts that have sizes you measured: brackets, enclosures, holders, a lid and a box, hole patterns. It needs more from you for a part that must fit a place you can only scan, and for an assembly of more than three or four parts that touch. It does not go well with organic shapes described in words alone, gears and threads written by hand, or sizes read from a photo. Whatever the part, give a measured number, a scan or a dimension mark in place of a description. The manual has the lists.

它是如何运作的

A workspace is a folder of projects. Each project is a folder with one build123d model in it:

projects/
├── bracket/
│   └── bracket.py
└── hollow/
    └── hollow.py

A model gives its parts as a dict, or as make_<part>() functions, or as module-level shapes:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from build123d import Box, Cylinder, Pos

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Params:
    side: float = 40
    wall: float = 2

def assembly(p):
    inner, height = p.side - 2 * p.wall, p.side - p.wall
    tub = Pos(0, 0, height / 2) * Box(p.side, p.side, height)
    tub -= Pos(0, 0, p.wall + inner / 2) * Box(inner, inner, inner)
    tub += Pos(0, 0, p.wall + 10) * Cylinder(3, 20)
    lid = Pos(0, 0, height + p.wall / 2) * Box(p.side, p.side, p.wall)
    return {"tub": tub, "lid": lid}

The app is Electron and three.js. The kernel is a Python package that loads models and tessellates them in forked workers. Each project gets its own Claude Code session, in the project's folder, connected to torno's MCP server on 127.0.0.1. See Projects and builds for the full rules.

入门

要求

  • Linux or macOS (not Windows: the launcher, the terminal view and the login-shell PATH are for Unix; WSL2 is untried)
  • Node.js 22.12 or later, and pnpm 10
  • uv (it fetches Python 3.11 or 3.12 if you have neither)
  • Claude Code (claude) on your PATH, logged in

torno checks all of this on its first screen, under "Ready to work", and says what's missing. The first build sets up torno's own Python environment with build123d and bd_warehouse (about 900 MB, once). If your workspace has its own pyproject.toml, torno uses that environment instead and never changes it. Run uv sync there once yourself. More in Requirements.

安装

git clone https://github.com/luisg0nc/torno.git
cd torno
pnpm install

Run

scripts/torno ~/projects    # open a folder as the workspace
scripts/torno               # the workspace you opened last, or the first screen

The launcher rebuilds the app when the sources change, so git pull and run it again. On the first screen, Open the example opens a small project, an enclosure with its brief and a few marks, in a temporary copy, so you can try everything without touching your own files.

On Linux, scripts/torno --install-desktop adds torno to your application launcher, or pnpm dist:linux builds an AppImage and a tar.gz in app/dist/. On macOS, pnpm dist:mac builds torno.app in app/dist/ (signed ad hoc, not notarized). More in Run.

Your first five minutes

Press Open the example on the first screen. It is an enclosure for a sensor board, with a lid that rattles. The manual has a walk-through on it: turning, pinning, measuring, cutting and asking the agent to fix the fit. It works the same from a packaged app.

Working with Claude Code in torno

A few habits that save time.

  • 点，不描述。 Pin the face and write the note. The agent gets the face's ref and your words, not "the left side near the top".
  • Give measured sizes. Put what you have measured in the brief or the first prompt. A size the agent guesses is the usual reason a part does not fit.
  • Make a dimension a standing test. Measure the wall or the gap, type the value it should have, and it says passes or fails after every build, whoever made the change.
  • Ask for two or three rough blockouts before details. Compare the shapes first. Fillets and holes can wait.
  • Ask for measured sizes back. "What is the wall under the lid?" is answered from the B-rep, exactly. Say so when you want the number and not a look.
  • Run /mcp__torno__review before you call it done. The agent goes through every open mark and every unmet dimension against the current build.
  • One project, a few parts. Split a big assembly into projects. Use saved views to come back to the same angle.

The manual says what the agent is given and told.

  • The manual, the reference for everything torno does. The parts most people need: The agent: the chat, what Claude Code is given and told, the tools Marks and measuring Scans and export Keys, files torno writes, troubleshooting
  • The design, why torno is built the way it is.
